newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran leader draws popular support at mass prayers.
newsitem.headline: Iran leader draws popular support at mass prayers.

text.p: Iranians crammed streets in central Tehran on Friday to hear supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei mark the first Friday prayer of the Islamic fasting month of Ramadan with a condemnation of Iran's Western enemies.

Khamenei, the spiritual heir of the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini who led Iran's 1979 Islamic revolution, addressed some 20,000 people at a former soccer pitch at Tehran university and to double this number through loudspeakers in nearby streets.
The mass audience, including senior state officials, clerics and wheelchair-bound veterans of the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war, sat silently but were roused when the state's enemies were evoked.
"Iran is victorious. America is defeated," came the crowd's response during the rare appearance by Khamenei at the university.
The Middle East peace process, America, Israel and neighbouring oil-rich states were all condemned with zeal as Khamenei portrayed a "psychological war" he said was being waged against Iran.
"If America and all world powers intend to pressure us, this nation will not back down...We shall not surrender," he said.
Iran-U.S. relations have entered a new downturn in recent months following hints by U.S. officials that Tehran may have had a role in a bombing in Saudi Arabia last June that killed 19 U.S. airmen.
Iran has not been officially linked to the bombing and the country has denied any role in the attack.
Diplomats and analysts say the United States might at some stage use its air superiority to strike at Iran if Washington were convinced that Iran played a role in the Saudi bombings.

If the prayers were any guide to the clerics' domestic strength almost 18 years after the revolution, it appeared Tehran's rulers could rely on sizeable popular support despite frequent reports in the local press about dissatisfacton over rising prices and unemployment.
Cars were parked nine-deep on the capital's wide roads.
Rows of women covered in black or white chadors and screened off from the men by blue canvas partitions, sat patiently on city streets while many young children sat by their fathers.

Under a steel roof at the former soccer pitch, war veterans -- many with severed limbs -- were treated by attendees to water from silver bowls while the exclusively male crowd lifted up their palms and prayed for the defence of the country.
"Please God save us from our enemy," Khamenei, wearing a black turban and thick glasses, said.
"Death to America. Death to Israel," came the response.
He addressed the crowds on the bright winter afternoon on an elavated platform covered by a banner with the words "Friday prayers are an example of loving and learning about Allah".

Security at the press box some seven metres from the leader was tight, not surprising as Khamenei lost the effective use of his right arm in the early 1980s after a bomb planted in a tape recorder exploded near him in a news conference.
